fullText:
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced that the US government would rename artificial intelligence "super intelligence" in official communications, as he firmly rejected calls for international supervision of AI, calling them a "globalist scheme" to control the new technology.

Speaking to the United Nations General Assembly, Trump argued the word "artificial" undersold the technology and voiced hope the rest of the world would adopt the new term.

"It sounds much better. It is much better, and it's much more accurate," he said.

The rebrand is the latest in a series of renamings pursued by the Trump administration, which changed the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America" via executive order last year and, in August, renamed Lake Ontario "Lake America" amid a trade dispute with Canada.

Trump has also floated renaming the Atlantic or Pacific oceans.

In his speech, Trump dismissed warnings from AI safety advocates, comparing them to warnings about climate change, whose human causes are affirmed by the overwhelming consensus of the scientific community.

"The United States totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control... artificial intelligence," he said.

"Every major new technology brings challenges, and superintelligence is no exception," he added.

"The very same people who said we'll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming... are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, and that everything is going to be a total disaster."

Ahead of the week of meetings and speeches in New York, leaders of more than 20 mostly European countries urged binding safety measures for advanced artificial intelligence, warning that the technology's development could outpace the ability to control it.

AI superpowers China and the United States did not endorse the idea.

The AI companies themselves are increasingly asking for global coordination on AI safety, with OpenAI's Sam Altman set to address the UN Security Council on Wednesday.

Anthropic chief Dario Amodei and Hugging Face co-founder Clement Delangue will also participate remotely, a French official said Tuesday.

France, which holds the Security Council presidency this month, initiated the meeting and believes AI's threat to international peace and security has not been sufficiently discussed at the council level.

UN chief Antonio Guterres, meanwhile, called for the US and China to start a dialogue on the technology's future akin to US-Soviet engagement at the height of the Cold War.

"Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation," Guterres said in his address to the assembly.

"At a pivotal moment during the Cold War, strategic rivals came to recognize the need to manage shared existential risks."

China and the US are currently discussing creating a communication channel for AI concerns in anticipation of a Washington summit meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

Both powers confront rising fears that increasingly capable artificial intelligence systems could eventually escape human control, even as they race for technological supremacy.

fullText:
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 22 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that Washington and Tehran were moving toward a settlement, while a senior Iranian official said Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the US eased military pressure and lifted its blockade on Iranian ports.

Trump's remarks came just hours after ‌he repeated a threat at the UN General Assembly to annihilate Iran if it failed to strike a deal.

Speaking after a meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the United Nations ‌in New York, Trump said: "They want to talk to us. They have been talking to us, even today they've been talking to us, and the relationship is developing.

"But we can't let them - and they understand that - we can't let them have a nuclear weapon."

He gave ​no details on the talks. No face-to-face meetings between Iran and the United States are known to have taken place since July, when an agreement on an interim deal to end the war collapsed weeks after it was signed.

Earlier, in a combative speech to the UN, Trump gave no sign of readiness to compromise. He called for Iran's complete economic isolation and said he believed a deal would be done after November's midterm elections "because it doesn't make sense for them not to. They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election."

Trump faces growing domestic discontent over the unpopular Iran war, rising energy costs and stubbornly elevated inflation.

Iran had earlier signalled a willingness to ‌revive negotiations to end their almost seven-month-old conflict, with the presidents of both ⁠countries due at the UN for the annual gathering.

The senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran had conveyed its latest proposal to Washington through mediators last week and could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to Gulf shipping within seven days if its demands were met.

IRAN SEES 'GOLDEN OPPORTUNITY' TO REVIVE DIPLOMACY

The official had earlier told Reuters that the ⁠US should "announce that it wants to resolve the issue diplomatically, make that official, and then agree on a timeline".

"The UN General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy," the official said.

In a reminder of Iran's firm position so far, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who headed Iran's negotiating team at previous talks, said Iran would never surrender: "Trump must understand that he cannot impose his power on the Iranian people and its armed forces."

Trump was due ​to ​meet on Tuesday with leaders of the six Gulf Arab states: Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab ​Emirates.

All are keen to restore shipping through Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of ‌global oil and gas shipments before the war, but wary of giving their longstanding rival Iran too much power.

All apart from Oman also host huge US military bases that have come under repeated Iranian attack throughout the war.

Saudi Arabia, the largest of the Gulf states, has been drawn deeper into the war this month as Iran-aligned Houthi fighters have advanced in Yemen, routing forces of the Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.

Oil markets found some relief on Tuesday after sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline and could resume exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu within hours, albeit at reduced volumes. [O/R]

The pipeline, Saudi Arabia's main export route bypassing wartime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, had been shut after attacks this month that Riyadh blamed on Iranian-backed groups in Iraq.

SAUDIS SEEK US SUPPORT AGAINST ‌HOUTHIS

The Houthis have driven back Saudi-supported government forces along the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its mouth, ​and have attacked Saudi Arabia directly with missiles and drones. They are now pushing to seize the strategic heights of the Kahboub ​Mountains that overlook the Red Sea coast.

The US, which bombed the Houthis for two months last ​year, has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to rejoin the fight. The New York Times reported that Trump called off US ‌strikes against the Houthis on Sunday at the last minute.

Asked why Washington had ​held back from striking the Houthis, US Secretary of State ​Marco Rubio said: "Ultimately, if it comes down to it, the United States will always stand with Saudi Arabia and support them because we have an agreement with them to do so.

"That said, that is a very dangerous and complex conflict that pre-exists ... We have a history with the Houthis as well, and that's something we don't want to see impacted either."

On the table at the Gulf ​states' meeting with Trump is a Qatari proposal for a framework to bring ‌Iran and the Arab Gulf states into a common security architecture, regional sources said. One source said Iran was reviewing the proposal.

Speaking at the Qatar Economic Forum in New York on ​Sunday, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said any such arrangement would need to provide security guarantees for the Gulf states and expand economic interdependence with Iran.

(Reporting ​by Reuters Gulf bureaux;Writing by Peter Graff and Kevin Liffey; Editing by Gareth Jones, Alexandra Hudson, Ros Russell)

“Over the course of a lifetime, there are only so many real opportunities to make decisions that we know will shape our personal history and the history of those we live with and care about for a long time to come. This is one of those moments,” he said, before mentioning the Kennedy Center board’s attempts to inscribe Trump’s name on the historic Washington building.

Last week, a federal judge blocked an effort by the Trump-picked board to add the president’s name to the institution and to rename its campus after Trump.

“I personally think that the way we’ve argued about what’s going on at the Kennedy Center and all that kind of stuff — I think we’ve been majoring in the minors,” Clinton said.

“You really think 100 years from now anybody’s going to care very much about whose name’s on what building?” he asked.

“Isn’t it more important what happens in the building? And what happens outside the building?” he continued.

“I feel so strongly — as I did 30 years ago-plus when I ran for president as a virtual child — that diversity is a positive thing, not a negative one.”

“That cooperation works better than conflict, and that we could actually deal with just about every challenge we face, if we didn’t care as much about who got the credit, and we made sure that we took care of the least of these,” Clinton, 80, said.

His remarks largely focused on dealing with the development of artificial intelligence and criticizing “zero-sum thinking” by the country’s political leaders.

“I believe that on the 250th anniversary of this country, we can’t have a politics driven by zero-sum thinking: In order for me to win, you have to lose,” he said.

“Nevertheless, I do understand why so many leaders around the world have chosen this zero-sum approach. Think how richly they have been rewarded for it in every sense of the word, and this payoff has been more apparent in the United States than any other country,” the former commander in chief said.

“Some days I can hardly believe what is happening in this country that I love so much. People in charge have created one set of rules for themselves and another set for everyone else,” Clinton said, without mentioning Trump by name.

“They’ve weaponized government to settle personal scores, prosecute enemies, stamp out free speech. They’ve even made the federal government a new profit center for themselves and their allies,” he said.

“That violates the spirit and letter of the Emoluments Clause of our Constitution.”

title: Trump Wants to Keep Journalists Out of the White House. He Should Get His Wish.
description: Chris...
fullText:
The president has banned MS NOW, CNN, and Politico from attending press briefings. The rest of the media should respond with a boycott.

At a loss to assert persuasive control over the cooling economy, the dismal and nonsensical war in Iran, the runaway development of AI, or the food supply, President Donald Trump has reverted to the conservative movement’s go-to culture-war refrain: demonizing the media. In an overheated Truth Social post late last week, Trump announced that he was revoking the clearances of CNN, Politico, and MS NOW to continue attending White House briefings. Sure enough, reporters from those outlets found their access to the White House blocked when they tried to gain entry. The targeted news organizations have announced that they will sue the Trump administration for depriving them of basic First Amendment freedoms.

That action is a sound and time-honored line of defense for news outlets facing the specter of prior restraint from the executive branch. Yet Trump’s unconstitutional blacklist move—which he vowed would be but the opening salvo in his administration’s press inquisition—creates an opening to finally chloroform the desiccated ritual of the White House press briefing. The time is ripe for a full boycott of the Trump agitprop spectacle from every news organization in America. The decision by TV networks to suspend pool coverage of the White House is a good first step in this direction, but the simple truth of the matter is that the American press can only regain its independence by quitting the White House briefing room once and for all.

Like the embarrassingly compromised annual White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, the briefing has long outlived any notional journalistic purpose it might have once served. Going back to Ron Ziegler’s reign as enfant terrible of the messaging arm of the Nixon White House, the briefings have always functioned chiefly as culture-war theater, allowing presidents and press secretaries to browbeat correspondents for raising questions that contradict their ideological power scripts, while granting showboating network correspondents in the Sam Donaldson vein quick and viral opportunities to be seen haranguing administration flacks in a brightly lit intellectual vacuum. In many ways, Trump’s bid to limit exchanges in the briefing room to exercises in ideologically vetted rightthink is but the logical limit-case of the Faustian bargain that’s fueled the briefing room’s operations for decades.

Prior to Trump’s power grab, the Oval Office deference of the White House briefing reached its purest form in the George W. Bush White House, when the president made a point of icing out UPI correspondent Helen Thomas, a fierce critic of the invasion of Iraq, from any recognition from the podium for three years. That petulant display of favoritism spoke volumes about what the briefings were meant to accomplish: patrician indulgences for mainstream correspondents willing to toe the party line, and pariahdom for any hapless dissenter. For Bush, it worked—the White House press corps was content to sit on its hands as the administration treated Thomas like a dirty hippie, and they continued parroting the administration’s Iraq War fantasias to epically calamitous effect.

In his own vendetta against the White House press corps, Trump has merely turned this tactic up to 11, punishing any news outlet that has inadvertently stood athwart his own bottomless store of imagined grievance. (His decision to banish CNN is especially rich, since under the watch of its moronic former CEO Jeff Zucker the cable networked devoted acres of unfiltered coverage to Trump’s 2016 campaign—a virtual in-kind donation that worked out to roughly $2 billion across the industry, as other witless executives followed Zucker’s lead.)

Of course, the news organizations currently battling to reclaim their spots in the briefing room aren’t likely to sign on to the mission to abolish it altogether. Just for starters, they’d be loath to surrender the status and convenience of a perch within the White House—and TV news outfits in particular aren’t likely to surrender the cheap optics furnished by theatrical bantering with a president or his designated press flacks. But in substantive journalistic terms, there’s nothing to be gained by continuing this Kabuki theater of imperial press-corps respectability. Especially under an administration that has made the pursuit of empirical truth a de facto thought crime, no civic purpose is served by sending out network anchorbots en masse to field its lies. And once we’ve dispensed with the briefings, we can embark on a long-overdue recalibration of the logic of White House coverage.

Instead of passively conniving in the bid to remake the White House press corps in the image of Bari Weiss’s CBS News, news organizations can hold administration officials truly accountable by drawing on contributions from people who actually know something about key policy calls. In lieu of airing an endless regress of breathless will-they-won’t-they accounts of Federal Reserve rate hikes or focusing on Wall Street’s instant reaction, press outlets could have actual economists assess the likely impact of the Fed’s decision-making in the real economy. Or as Russell Vought seeks the authority to administer and strike down research grants at the National Institute of Health, news organizations can track the fallout on a whole series of fronts, from cancer treatments to public health to longevity. Climate journalists could, at long last, be in a position to foreground the global catastrophe that the Trump administration is fomenting by treating climate change as a hoax.

Major news organizations did refuse, after all, to take part in Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s effort to turn Pentagon press corps into an agitprop subsidiary, and there’s been no fall-off in crucial coverage of his woeful term in office. Indeed, GOP Representative Thomas Massie’s motion to impeach Hegseth, which spooked MAGA-prostrate House Speaker Mike Johnson into calling the chamber into an early fall recess, drew extensively on press accounts that documented Hegseth’s unfitness for office in scarifying detail, from the Defense Department’s campaign of murder in the Southern Hemisphere to the Pentagon’s shameful effort to conceal American fatalities in the Iran war. Let the members of the White House press corps heed this example, and start exercising actual journalistic independence—together with the ability to genuinely think and research for themselves.

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

We must have an independent media that sets the record straight, unearths corruption and abuses of power, and advances a politics of justice and dignity for all if we’re to win this fight.

That’s why I’m writing to you today. This September, The Nation needs to add 100 monthly donors to sustain our progressive journalism. Your contribution makes the next investigative report, the next truth-speaking column, and the next pathbreaking essay all possible. 

I hope you’ll support our work with a recurring donation today. If you donate $10 or more a month, we’ll send you a brand new “Hands Off the Free Press!” sticker to recognise your commitment to our cause. Please, donate today.

Onward,

Katrina vanden Heuvel
Editor and Publisher, The Nation

title: Trump, Greenland and Denmark to sign deal in bid to end Arctic standoff
description:

   COPENHAGEN, Sept 22 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump is due to meet with leaders of Greenland and Denmark on Tuesday to sign a deal that will allow a larger ‌US military presence on Greenland and could end a standoff over the strategically located and ‌mineral-rich island. 
   The agreement will allow the US to expand its military footprint in Greenland, three people familiar with the matter have told ​Reuters. 
   In addition to the existing Pituffik Space Base, the deal is expected to open two new military sites: Narsarsuaq, a former Cold War airbase whose population has dwindled to just a few dozen, and Mestersvig, currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, an elite Danish special forces unit. 
   Greenland, a former colony and now a semi-autonomous ‌territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, ⁠sits between the Arctic and North America and holds vast energy resources. 
   Trump's refusal to rule out military or economic force to acquire it triggered a diplomatic crisis in ⁠January within NATO and forced Denmark and the island's government into intensive negotiations.
fullText:
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 22 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump and the leaders of ‌Greenland and Denmark signed an agreement on Tuesday that ‌permits a larger US military presence on Greenland and may resolve a ​standoff over the strategically located and mineral-rich island.

The agreement, signed during Trump's visit to the UN General Assembly in New York, stops short of Trump's demand that the US adopt Greenland as ‌a US territory to ⁠head off the growing Arctic presence of Russia and China.

But the deal does permit a greater ⁠US military presence on the icy territory, an option that emerged as Greenland leaders argued against a complete US takeover.

In his ​speech to ​the assembled world leaders at ​the UN before the signing ‌ceremony, Trump said the agreement gives the US "permanent control over security and all other needs on that territory."

"No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland any more, or make sensitive investments there without our express ‌written approval," Trump said.

Trump signed the ​agreement along with Danish Prime Minister ​Mette Frederiksen and Greenland ​Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen in a trilateral ceremony ‌after Trump gave his UN ​speech.

Frederiksen described the ​agreement as "a deal that can "last forever" and said it underlines the importance of the NATO alliance and respects Greenland's ​right to self-determination.

(Reporting ‌by Gram Slattery at the UN and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen ​in Copenhagen; Writing by Steve Holland; Editing Xevi Fontdegloria, ​Ross Colvin and Rosalba O'Brien)

fullText:
President Donald Trump's push to convert his planned triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery into a military complex has complicated a required federal review process and raised new legal and safety concerns.

Trump unveiled his new national security rationale Sunday in a post on Truth Social, saying that the 250-foot-tall arch project - which he has framed for nearly a year as a tourist attraction - will now house drones, snipers and ammunition. The president said he was making the change at the request of the U.S. military.

Critics of the plan saw echoes of Trump's shifting security case for the White House ballroom, which the administration has used to defend that project in court. But while presidents have historically had some leeway to revamp the White House grounds, the arch would stand on federal parkland more than a mile away, where Congress has set stricter rules for construction.

"There is nothing that authorizes or justifies a massive arch, even if Trump tries to disguise it as a military facility," said Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on a House committee that oversees federal parkland. "This is cartoonishly illegal, but he's obviously trying to find a way to do it anyway."

Aviation experts warned Monday that using drones at the planned arch site - Memorial Circle, a roundabout near Reagan National Airport - could pose risks in the airport's crowded airspace.

"Anything you add to the airspace complicates the airspace and increases the operational risk," said Tom Lintner, a former safety official at the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

Other military and safety experts have questioned the implications of storing ammunition in the middle of a heavily used traffic circle and whether tourists could still enter the arch as previously planned.

Historic preservationists participating in a required federal review process said they could not move forward until the administration clarifies Trump's plans for the arch. Administration officials last week had asked Washington and Virginia's preservation offices to agree to a memorandum of agreement (MOA) by Monday as part of that process, and they invited other preservationists to participate.

"This MOA is DOA," Charles Birnbaum of the Cultural Landscape Foundation wrote in an email to the administration on Monday. An official for Washington's historic preservation office also wrote in an email that the office needed clarity on Trump's post. Both emails were shared with The Washington Post.

Administration officials have declined to offer further details about Trump's plans to convert the arch to a military complex. They have previously said that they will not begin construction on the arch until they have received "all necessary approvals."

But Trump has pushed his deputies to expedite the arch and other construction projects, particularly in the wake of a Supreme Court ruling on Aug. 31 that let him continue building his ballroom, according to two people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations. The ruling did not decide the merits of the case.

Spokespeople for the White House and Pentagon said on Monday that they had no additional information to provide beyond the president's social media post. A defense official, speaking on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue, said it was not clear if U.S. Northern Command, which oversees domestic military operations, has been asked to develop any related plans.

Military officials with Joint Task Force-National Capital Region, which oversees military operations to protect D.C., did not respond to requests for comment on Monday. Spokespeople for the Interior Department and the National Park Service also did not respond to questions about the project. The Federal Aviation Administration referred questions to the White House.

Until Sunday, the Trump administration had largely portrayed the arch as a prominent tourist attraction. Architectural plans posted by the National Park Service last month include a "ticket booth," a "family restroom" and other features atypical of any active military complex.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum mentioned that the arch would also offer a "military observation deck" in a social media post earlier this month.

The administration had already faced safety questions, in part because the 250-foot-tall structure would sit directly in National Airport flight paths. Aviation safety there has garnered significant attention since a 2025 collision between an Army helicopter and an American Airlines regional jet near the airport that killed 67 people.

On Friday, the FAA said it had determined that the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft, including at National Airport. That finding preceded Trump's announcement about drones, whose type and frequency of use remain unclear.

In its final study on the arch, the FAA said the proposed structure should feature "a nonstandard eternal flame" to make it noticeable to pilots. It also said the arch should be continuously floodlighted by searchlight projectors around its base.

Jeff Guzzetti, a former FAA and National Transportation Safety Board accident investigator, said having drones in the flight path of National would worsen the airport's congestion problem.

"Even not knowing how often these things are going to be used, it would certainly increase the risk of a collision with a commercial airliner," Guzzetti said.

Michael McCormick, coordinator of the Air Traffic Management program at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, said he expected the FAA would need to conduct another study.

"Whatever the drones are, no matter what, the FAA would have to approve their flight because it's civilian airspace," McCormick said. "It cannot be a unilateral decision by the Pentagon."

fullText:
The fallout from President Trump's decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from the White House continued on Monday, with the news organizations filing a federal lawsuit, other outlets dropping their coverage in protest and the administration launching a live YouTube stream branded "TRUMP TV."

In response to the ban, four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — refused to participate in the White House pool, the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events. CNN had been scheduled to serve as the television pool on Monday.

As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone that the pool would typically provide.

On Monday night, the White House launched a Trump TV YouTube stream. Branded "TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station," the White House said in its description that it would run videos and highlights of "the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place." The first video showed Trump's remarks on July 3 at Mount Rushmore.

The three banned news organizations filed a lawsuit against Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court earlier Monday, demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in a joint statement. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

According to the complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House are retaliating against them for coverage they dislike.

"President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration," the complaint states. "But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting."

The organizations argue that their reporters were not afforded due process and are asking a federal judge to quickly rule that Trump's ban is unconstitutional. The filing cites a 1977 ruling by the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which found that the White House cannot arbitrarily deny a journalist a press pass without due process.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the filing states.

Trump appeared to respond to the lawsuit in a social media post early Monday.

"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America," the president wrote on Truth Social. "It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!"

A hearing was set for Wednesday. Trump indicated in a follow-up Truth Social post that he would appeal any ruling against him.

The White House released a statement on Monday afternoon, saying that access for journalists is "a privilege — not a right."

"The First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool," the statement read. "No President is required to host a hostile operation on the grounds. Access has always been a privilege — and President Trump is applying that rule."

On Friday afternoon, Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post, saying it was not prompted by any particular stories but was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said at an Oval Office event an hour later while explaining his decision to enact "the ban on the free press."

"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories," the president said. "If they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house."

According to CNN, Trump's close aide Natalie Harp showed him clips of media coverage shortly before he announced the ban.

On Saturday, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were turned away from the White House by members of the Secret Service and had their credentials — so-called hard passes needed for access — confiscated.

The journalists — CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett — are listed as plaintiffs in the court filing.

The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the move, saying it violates the First Amendment.

"The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News senior White House correspondent and WHCA president, said in a statement. "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."

On Sunday, Trump posted what appeared to be an AI-generated image of trash bags bearing the logos of CNN, MSNBC (MS NOW's former name) and Politico outside the White House.

The three news outlets are longstanding members of the White House press pool that provides rotating coverage of the administration and travels with the president.

The daily guidance issued by the White House for Monday listed no primary TV pool, identifying Hearst and Real America's Voice as the "secondary" TV crews for the president's events in Washington and his scheduled trip to New York City for the United Nations General Assembly.

The Washington Post, the New York Times and HuffPost each announced that they would not publish images of Trump's trip on Monday in solidarity with the banned journalists.

U.S. presidents throughout history have complained about negative coverage of their administrations. In 2009, the Obama administration sought to exclude Fox News from a series of interviews with a Treasury Department official in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, but backed down when the other major television networks objected.

Trump, however, has continued his adversarial relationship with the media, often referring to the press as the "enemy of the people."

In 2018, Trump administration officials revoked the press pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta after they said that he had interrupted the president during a news conference. The network sued, and a federal judge ordered Acosta's credentials restored.

A similar situation played out the following year when the White House revoked Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's press pass over a verbal argument between Karem and Sebastian Gorka, a former White House aide, at a Rose Garden event. A federal judge ordered the White House to restore Karem's pass.

Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some official events after the news service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In his first event without a network TV pool on Monday, Trump unveiled the White House's new helipad before departing for New York. His remarks were nearly inaudible on the White House video feed. Joe Reberkenny, a White House correspondent for the Washington Blade who was serving as the in-town pool reporter, said he couldn't hear Trump "over the sound of the helicopter."

fullText:
President Donald Trump gave his highly anticipated U.N. General Assembly speech Tuesday morning in front of a standing room only crowd.

However, as Trump spoke about the last six months of Iran military strikes, that country's U.N. delegates walked out of the assembly.

Trump told the gathering of world leaders in New York City said that he had a "big decision" coming up on Iran.

“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” Trump asked.

“Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?” The president continued: “Do I drive them into hell?”

Trump said he believes Tehran will “make a deal right after the [midterm] election” in November.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi are in New York for the annual meeting but didn’t attend Trump’s speech. However, their staff and delegates watched the beginning of Trump's speech then exited the General Assembly 10 minutes into his remarks. Only one Iranian delegate remained in the hall to listen to the U.S. president.

As Trump spoke about Iran, the camera panned to the lone remaining delegate from Iran, who glared stone-faced at the president.

Newsweek reached out to the Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs via email on Tuesday morning for comment.

Trump also said in his speech that he's not concerned about the war in Iran hurting Republicans in the midterm elections.

The election “doesn’t even enter my mind” when it comes to Iran, he said.

A new NBC News poll found widespread skepticism toward the conflict, with 62 percent of voters saying the war has not been worth it and 57 percent saying they would be less likely to support candidates who back it. The findings arrive amid growing Republican unease over the war's political costs, particularly in competitive midterm races.

Diesel has risen to a record $6.50 amid ongoing supply constraints from the Iran war and other global pressures, exposing a significant political vulnerability for the GOP.

Still, Trump said he’s not concerned with politics.

“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election,” Trump said of Iran. “What they don’t realize is that I’m not running. I did that already, and won in a landslide … and I’ll be here for two-and-a-half years.”

President Trump lashed out at CNN's Kaitlan Collins before his address the U.N. General Assembly in New York amid the White House ban to deny CNN, MS NOW and Politico access.

Those three news outlets are suing the president for violating the First Amendment.

Collins asked Trump as he entered the U.N. building, "Two thirds of Americans don't think the U.S. is winning the war with Iran. When will it end?"

Arriving with First Lady Melania Trump, Trump brushed aside the question and told Collins: "You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me. You shouldn't be covering me."

After Trump's comments, Collins said on CNN that the network "never said we were not going to cover the president" and vowed that CNN would continue reporting on him despite the White House's efforts to restrict its access. She noted that the network was covering the president from the United Nations under U.N. credentials while the legal fight over White House access continues.

This is a breaking news article. Updates to follow.

The Associated Press contributed to this story.

And there’s no mention of Britain backing compulsory pre-release testing of AI, unlike the other countries. The language in the press release is much more watery: he wants to ensure AI is used “for good” but avoids specifics.

Darren Jones, chief secretary to the PM when Keir Starmer was in Downing Street, has said the government should not be shunning this initiative. He says:

It’s great to see @alexstubb providing this leadership and bringing other countries together to call for pre-deployment testing.

The list of signatories to the ‘Call for Control of Frontier AI Models’ are the United Kingdom’s natural allies.

The UK has special access to American AI models through the AI Security Institute, which is partly why the UK Government will want to remain in lock step with the United States.

But I don’t see any reason why the UK can’t I encourage our government to do so and to offer to broker agreement on its application with the United States.

The comment from Andy Burnham criticising Donald Trump from 2017 quoted earlier (see 9.58am) referred to the prospect of Trump visiting Manchester during his state visit. In fact, he never went near the city. But next year he may be there, because No 10 has announced that it will host the G20 summit.

In its report on the story, the Manchester Evening News says:

The move to host the G20 in Manchester was reportedly set up months ago after Andy Burnham became prime minister, using his first phone call with Mr Trump to invite him to the city, and which is said to have been accepted by the American President.

It is understood that planning has already started for the enormous gathering, which will require the biggest security operation the city has ever seen …

Work on hosting the summit in Manchester had begun before Mr Burnham took office but the prime minister has been an enthusiastic cheerleader for the city since entering Downing Street, including establishing the No 10 North operation in the city centre.

In his huddle on the plane to the US, Andy Burnham also confirmed that the UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters. He said:

We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling.

Presumably that means Burnham won’t be agreeing with the recent report from the Campaign Against Arms Trade and the Transition Security Project saying “Britain should pay reparations to the people of Yemen for its role in crimes committed against them by Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and their coalition allies during the Yemeni civil war.” It says:

Speaking to journalists on his flight to New York, Andy Burnham played down suggestions that previous critical things he has said about Donald Trump could cause a problem when they meet later.

As with almost everyone on the left of politics in the UK, Burnham has a longish record of saying disobliging things about the US president. In 2017, as mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham said that as a “matter of principle” he would not meet Trump because of the “hateful, extremist material” he posted online. After Trump backed his supporters who stormed the US Capitol on 6 January 2021 to try to overturn the presidential election result, Burnham said: “Any UK politician who gave Trump the time of day should be ashamed right now.” Only last year he accused Trump of bringing “instability to the world”.

Burnham did not apologise for any of these comments, or retract them, but he told reporters it was time to move on. He also pointed out that Trump had been dismissive of him recently, describing him as “the mayor of a town”.

Politicians say things throughout their career, but now the important thing is to focus on the moment you are in, and I did say to the president in our first phone call, I said Mr President, Manchester isn’t ‘some town’. I said ‘this is Manchester’.

And so yes, the right thing to do is to have a laugh about it, isn’t it, and move beyond it.

Asked if he could trust Trump, Burnham said:

When you come into this job, you realise how deep this relationship is. We trust our allies. Of course, we do.

Asked if he trusted Trump personally, Burnham replied: “Yes.”

(This is one of those comments best understood by applying the Mandy Rice-Davies principle, rather than taking it literally.)

Politico has a bit more colour on the huddle in today’s London Playbook.

Burnham’s first huddle with the Lobby pack on the government jet, where he sat chatting for 38 minutes in jeans, a suit jacket and his blue Joseph’s Goal wristband. It was a more discursive affair than under Starmer. The newbie PM was so disappointed that no hacks asked him to diss Danny Dyer — see here for the very sweary context— that he volunteered the line anyway. “I’m not sure I know who he is,” said Burnham. “Is he the father-in-law of a West Ham player?”

Andy Burnham has opened the door to fighting the next election on the UK rejoining the EU, but said his immediate priority was continuing to rebuild bridges with European allies. Pippa Crerar has the story, which is based on what Burnham told journalists as he spoke to them in what reporters call a “huddle” on his flight to New York.

Good morning. Andy Burnham is at the United Nations general assembly today and in a speech to the world (or, technically, to people in the hall and anyone watching on TV at around 2am UK time), he will say that Britain is not “on the slide”.

Speaking to reporters on the plane to New York, Burnham said:

The plan for Britain is about ‘what is our direction over the next 10 years and how do we make life more affordable for people’. That is my main priority, that’s what people are looking for.

I hear people saying the country is on the slide – we’re the fastest growing in the G7, there’s lots to be proud of, there’s a lot right with the country and I’m going to give a really upbeat message when I speak.

But the story of the day will instead focus on Burnham’s meeting with someone who does think the UK is “on the slide”, or at least claims to think that. “Your country’s in trouble. You’re on the edge of disaster,” Donald Trump told a GB News reporter recently.

In her overnight story ahead of the meeting, Pippa Crerar, who is on the trip with Burnham, says Burnham is going to adopt a middle-of-the-road approach to the US president when they meet. She says:

Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as [Keir] Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality.

This is a reference to Starmer offering Trump an unprecedented second state visit when they first met at the White House. Theresa May also found herself pimping the monarch at her first meeting with Trump. There were good reasons for both offers at the time, and they bought both newbie PMs some goodwill from the White House monster, but it did not last and both those encounters are now recalled as moments of national embarrassment. As long as today’s meeting is cordial, Burnham will probably be happy with something more low-key.

It is hard to know what can be achieved in any meeting with Trump because he is so unpredicable. Later Burnham has another meeting with a president which will get far less coverage, but may turn out to be more consequential. The PM is meeting Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, for the first time and, with the prospects of the EU-UK reset in jeopardy, there is a lot to discuss.

Here is the agenda for the day.

9am: The final day of the Lib Dem conference in Brighton starts. The debates this morning will include one on the Lib Dems’ water policy.

2.30pm: Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, gives his keynote speech at the conference.

Around 4.45pm (UK time): Andy Burnham is due to meet Donald Trump at the UN in New York.

Late afternoon/early evening (UK time): Burnham has bilateral meetings with Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, and others.

Late evening (UK time): Burnham co-chairs a meeting on the Middle East with other leaders including Emmanuel Macron, the French president, and Mark Carney, the Canadian PM.

Around 1.50am (UK time): Burnham gives his speech to the UN before flying back to the UK.

fullText:
US President Donald Trump is expected to claim he is winning both on the battlefield and as a peacemaker Tuesday in a speech to the United Nations overshadowed by growing spillover from his stalled war against Iran.

Trump will likely not hold back in renewing his frequent boasts that under him the United States is "the hottest country" in the world.

He is also expected to seek to justify the Iran war, which has so far failed to fulfil White House objectives and provoked widespread economic damage over the Strait of Hormuz's closure.

But the self-styled peacemaker could equally use the UN stage to tout his controversial efforts to end the Gaza conflict and his ongoing effort to bring more Arab countries into the Abraham Accords with Israel.

"No one knows what Trump is going to say, not even Trump's speechwriters," International Crisis Group's Daniel Forti said.

"This year, we expect more of a contrast between Trump, sort of both announcing and celebrating his record as a peacemaker versus defending his ongoing military operations around the world," said Forti.

"It's not entirely clear what reaction Trump's going to get from world leaders."

The keynote speech at the start of the UN General Assembly High-level week will provide Trump with a big platform to renew his frequent assaults on the global body.

Last year's speech was characterized by Trump's extraordinary accusations of UN sabotage when an escalator in the New York headquarters briefly stopped working and the teleprompter glitched.

Trump has regularly attacked the UN and its leader Antonio Guterres since returning to office, although Washington last week reportedly paid $725 million into its budget, avoiding the embarrassment of losing some of its voting rights.

He is also likely to meet skepticism over his claims of a historic win for the United States when a security deal is signed Tuesday for a US presence in Greenland -- a territory of Denmark that Trump repeatedly threatened, driving bitter divisions through longtime US-led alliances.

As well as his closely watched speech to the General Assembly, Trump will hold side meetings with Britain's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, as well as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Japanese premier Sanae Takaichi and Venezuela's interim leader Delcy Rodriguez.

Rodriguez has governed under intense American pressure since her predecessor Nicolas Maduro was captured by US forces in January.

Last year, Trump's speech to the gathering of world leaders veered into a rant about an escalator that stalled as he was using it, suggesting it was done deliberately.

He also railed against a defective teleprompter, falsely accused London's mayor of imposing Islamic law and said Europe was in "serious trouble" over migration.

Trump clearly has not gotten over the incidents.

"They turned off the escalator," Trump said last week in the Oval Office.

"Fortunately, my first lady was very strong and I was able to grab her back or another part of her body. It was actually a little bit lower than the back," he said.

The offending escalator "has been checked and rechecked," Guterres's spokesman Stephane Dujarric said Monday.

"New arrangements were made to facilitate the US delegation's use of a teleprompter, they now have a separate booth, so we hope that will work without a hitch," he added.

Guterres, who kicks off the week of speeches, is expected to touch on the explosion of artificial intelligence and the multiple wars raging globally.

Next up -- just before Trump -- will be Brazilian President Lula Inacio Lula da Silva, whose country by tradition is always first to speak at the annual gathering of leaders.

Trump, who has supported Lula's opponents and other right-wing candidates across Latin America, may not like what he hears.

Leftist Lula, running for reelection, said last week that he would tell Trump to not "meddle" in Brazil's upcoming vote.

title: 'Blatant violation' of rights: News outlets file lawsuit over Trump ban

The three banned news organizations filed a lawsuit against Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court earlier Monday, demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored.
fullText:
A growing list of news organizations has announced that they will not publish photographs from the White House on Monday in response to President Trump's move last week to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from covering him or his administration in person.

The Washington Post, the New York Times and HuffPost each announced Monday afternoon that they were joining the four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — in refusing to participate in the White House pool, the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events.

As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone that the pool would typically provide.

Later in the day, the White House announced the creation of Trump TV, though details on what the service might include weren't provided.

The three banned news organizations filed a lawsuit against Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court earlier Monday, demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in a joint statement. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

CNN had been scheduled to serve as the television pool on Monday. According to Politico, the four other major TV networks are declining to participate in White House pool duties moving forward in response to the ban.

According to the complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House are retaliating against them for coverage they dislike.

"President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration," the complaint states. "But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting."

The organizations argue that their reporters were not afforded due process and are asking a federal judge to quickly rule that Trump's ban is unconstitutional. The filing cites a 1977 ruling by the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which found that the White House cannot arbitrarily deny a journalist a press pass without due process.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the filing states.

Trump appeared to respond to the lawsuit in a social media post early Monday.

"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America," the president wrote on Truth Social. "It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!"

The White House released a statement on Monday afternoon, saying that access for journalists is "a privilege — not a right."

"The First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool," the statement read. "No President is required to host a hostile operation on the grounds. Access has always been a privilege — and President Trump is applying that rule."

On Friday afternoon, Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post, saying it was not prompted by any particular stories but was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said at an Oval Office event an hour later while explaining his decision to enact "the ban on the free press."

"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories," the president said. "If they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house."

According to CNN, Trump's close aide Natalie Harp showed him clips of media coverage shortly before he announced the ban.

On Saturday, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were turned away from the White House by members of the Secret Service and had their credentials — so-called hard passes needed for access — confiscated.

The journalists — CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett — are listed as plaintiffs in the court filing.

The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the move, saying it violates the First Amendment.

"The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News senior White House correspondent and WHCA president, said in a statement. "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."

On Sunday, Trump posted what appeared to be an AI-generated image of trash bags bearing the logos of CNN, MSNBC (MS NOW's former name) and Politico outside the White House.

The three news outlets are longstanding members of the White House press pool that provides rotating coverage of the administration and travels with the president.

The daily guidance issued by the White House for Monday listed no primary TV pool, identifying Hearst and Real America's Voice as the "secondary" TV crews for the president's events in Washington and his scheduled trip to New York City for the United Nations General Assembly. Trump is scheduled to meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday afternoon.

U.S. presidents throughout history have complained about negative coverage of their administrations. In 2009, the Obama administration sought to exclude Fox News from a series of interviews with a Treasury Department official in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, but backed down when the other major television networks objected.

Trump, however, has continued his adversarial relationship with the media, often referring to the press as the "enemy of the people."

In 2018, Trump administration officials revoked the press pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta after they said that he had interrupted the president during a news conference. The network sued, and a federal judge ordered Acosta's credentials restored.

A similar situation played out the following year when the White House revoked Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's press pass over a verbal argument between Karem and Sebastian Gorka, a former White House aide, at a Rose Garden event. A federal judge ordered the White House to restore Karem's pass.

Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some official events after the news service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In his first event without a network TV pool on Monday, Trump unveiled the White House's new helipad before departing for New York. His remarks were nearly inaudible on the White House video feed. Joe Reberkenny, a White House correspondent for the Washington Blade who was serving as the in-town pool reporter, said he couldn't hear Trump "over the sound of the helicopter."

fullText:
Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.

“If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Monday, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency.

Mohebbi did not provide details on what the new weapons were or which new locations could be hit.

Earlier, Trump said he would “probably” be open to meeting with his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, during the United Nations General Assembly this week, Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reported Sunday.

The possibility of a meeting offered a glimmer of hope for a resolution to the nearly seven-month war with Iran, which has resulted in Iran blocking the key Strait of Hormuz, and its Yemeni allies bombing a crucial east-west oil pipeline and threatening another crucial waterway. Resultant economic shock waves have hit the U.S. and the world economy, driving up oil and diesel prices and fueling inflation.

Trump also said he was still deciding how to proceed with the war, describing his options as “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically, or making a deal.”

“My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up,” he said.

“They better behave,” Trump warned.

The president has previously said he did not believe the Iran war would end until after November’s midterm elections. He has also said oil prices would not come down until then.

Oil prices slid to their lowest point in more than a week Monday as hopes for renewed talks between the U.S. and Iran grew, while signs of a recovery in Saudi crude exports eased supply concerns, despite continued attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis.

Trump told Fox News that Washington was in constant communication with the Houthis — and that the Yemeni rebel group had agreed not to fight with the U.S., Yingst reported.

Trump has said that the administration had been in touch with the Houthis, but did not say when.

“The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through.”

Violence escalated over the weekend, with the Houthis saying they had used missiles and drones to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh on Saturday, as well as an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub.

Meanwhile, fighting flared in southwest Yemen as the rebel group made gains against Saudi-backed forces.

The New York Times reported Monday that the president had considered, but ultimately decided against on Sunday joining Saudi Arabia in joint strikes against the Houthis in Yemen.

NBC News was not immediately able to independently confirm the newspaper’s reporting. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“This is a really fluid situation,” Adam Baron, a fellow at the New America think tank who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region, said Monday.

He cautioned that he would not “rule out anything” when it comes to Trump’s stance on whether to help Saudi Arabia in its fight against the Houthis.

Shipping data showed 17 commodity vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, down from 37 a week earlier, though Middle Eastern producers continue to export oil on tankers with their transponders off, Reuters reported.

A total of 22 tankers, mainly very large crude carriers, or VLCCs, exited Hormuz in the week of Sept. 13, with Saudi Arabia and Iraq each accounting for 43% of the volume, the outlet reported, citing data from tracking group Kpler, which maintains the MarineTraffic website.

Meanwhile, at least 51 vessels made the crossing along the Bab el Mandeb, with 33 vessels exiting the waterway over the weekend as the Houthis tightened their grip over the strait, the outlet reported. That was down from 57 vessels in the previous weekend.

The Yemeni Health and Environment Ministry accused Saudi Arabia of launching airstrikes targeting telecommunications towers in the Khabb wa ash-Sha’af district of Al-Jawf Governorate on Sunday that killed four telecommunications workers and injured three others.

“Targeting essential service infrastructure, including telecommunications towers, constitutes a flagrant violation of international and humanitarian laws,” the ministry said in a post on Telegram. “It reveals the aggressor’s determination to disrupt basic services and exacerbate the suffering of the Yemeni people,” it said.

fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump's trip to New York for a speech at the United Nations started Monday with a detour to Gracie Mansion for an hourlong chat — and a trip down memory lane — with Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

The president, appearing with Mamdani after their meeting, reminisced about his previous visits to the official residence of the city's mayors and recalled "great ones and some not so great ones" who have led the city in the past.

"Hopefully you're going to be a great one," he said, giving Mamdani a pat on the back. "And you're off to a start."

The meeting was the latest cordial encounter between the Republican president and a democratic socialist mayor, who have struck up a surprisingly warm relationship despite their lack of political overlap, and have tried to find common ground in helping the city they both love.

With scores of world leaders arriving in the city for the United Nations General Assembly, there Trump stood beside Mamdani on the lawn of the custard-yellow mayoral mansion in Manhattan.

"I have a lot of meetings right now, very important meetings with heads of different countries, but this is like a little bit of old home week for me," Trump said, adding "We've done so many things from the beautiful home or house or building standing right behind me."

Trump and Mamdani told reporters they discussed a potential housing project in the borough of Queens and how to make New York more affordable for the working class.

They have met at least twice previously and have appeared to maintain some level of contact with one another, though the mayor stays tightlipped about any ongoing conversations with the president.

The pair of polarizing leaders first gathered in the Oval Office shortly after Mamdani's election victory last year for a surprisingly cordial confab that centered on ways to help their shared hometown, a detente that came after months of verbal sparring.

A few months later in February, Mamdani again took a quick jaunt to Washington to present Trump with a mock New York Daily News front page that said "Trump to City: Let's Build," as he pitched new housing investments in the city.

As they did after their first Oval Office meeting, Trump and Mamdani acknowledged their political and policy differences while standing side by side.

Mamdani was asked about Trump's decision to bar certain news outlets from the White House, with the mayor saying it was important that those networks, and others, be present for the Gracie Mansion event. Trump then defended his restrictions on the news organizations whose coverage he called biased.

"It's interesting because they said they were gonna boycott me. But they never boycott me," the president said, before adding, "I think that these outlets have an obligation to be fair."

Trump's previous visits to Gracie Mansion included attending the 2003 wedding of former Mayor Rudy Giuliani and a 2007 book party for former Democratic U.S. Rep. Charles Rangel.

After Trump left, Mamdani returned to the lawn to answer a few more questions, telling reporters that he and the president have sharp disagreements but that the relationship has endured nevertheless.

"I will continue to have conversations with the president, and frankly, anyone who can deliver relief to the people of this city," Mamdani said.

title: Trump called off Houthi strikes as military leaders debated risks of expanding war
description:
President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House last week. (Samuel Corum / Bloomberg via Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — U.S. military leaders are divided on whether President Donald Trump should get involved with the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to two U.S.
fullText:
WASHINGTON — U.S. military leaders are divided on whether President Donald Trump should get involved with the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to two U.S. officials.

The Saudis have been asking Trump for the U.S. military to take action against the Houthis, a request that grew more urgent in recent days as the rebels claimed they shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet and were quickly advancing on Marib province, which is home to Yemen’s largest oil and gas fields.

Some military leaders are making the case within the Pentagon and to Trump administration officials that opening another military front in the region is a bad idea amid concerns about the Pentagon’s dwindling supply of defensive and long-range weaponry, while noting that the Houthis are not striking U.S. ships, the U.S. officials said.

Yet other military leaders are arguing in favor of strikes, saying the U.S. should help Riyadh retaliate for Houthi strikes in Saudi Arabia and the claim of downing of the F-15 — a challenge to Saudi air superiority over Yemen, the officials said. They said these military leaders are privately expressing concern that for the U.S. not to act more forcefully is a betrayal of an important regional ally.

Trump had ordered strikes against the Houthis to begin around 5 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on Sunday, but the military was notified shortly after 2 p.m. on Sunday that the order was canceled, the two U.S. officials said. One of the officials said Trump has not taken military action off the table in the future.

One senior U.S. military leader in the region specifically warned that action against the Houthis could create unmitigated risk to U.S. troops in Middle East and the Iran war mission, including a U.S. naval blockade and security operations in the Strait of Hormuz, the two U.S. officials said. They said the military leader also made clear that U.S. forces could carry out the Iran mission and strikes against the Houthis and mitigate some of the risks, the officials said.

The internal divide underscores the bind the president is increasingly in as the U.S. remains locked in a war with Iran that he began but has struggled to end, and faces a shortage of key weaponry. The Saudis have been a critical U.S. ally in the Middle East, including throughout the war with Iran. Trump told Fox News over the weekend that he’s deciding whether to escalate the war with Iran, a position he has articulated on and off over the past few months.

The White House and a spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in Washington, D.C., did not respond to a request for comment. The Pentagon declined to comment.

There has already been tension between the U.S. and its Middle East allies over the war. In May, Saudi Arabia was surprised by an announcement by Trump to help ships through the Strait of Hormuz and suspended the U.S. military’s ability to use its bases and airspace. Trump abruptly reversed his decision.

The U.S. has already been supporting the Saudis by sharing intelligence, helping with planning, sending military advisers forward with the Saudi forces and even providing some logistical support, NBC News has reported. But the Saudis have repeatedly asked the U.S. to do more, including help with strikes against the Houthis.

Trump had not shown interest in acting until Thursday, when Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman told him in a phone call that the kingdom cannot succeed alone and after a series of developments — including the Houthis targeting Saudi infrastructure, downing the F-15 and threatening to take control of Yemen’s oil industry, according to one of the U.S. officials.

After the call, Trump ordered the military to provide him with fresh options for strikes against the Houthis, the official said. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Dan Caine called a 6 p.m. emergency meeting in The Tank, the top-security conference room in the Pentagon, to discuss options, the official said, canceling a trip to Copenhagen to meet with NATO chiefs of defense.

U.S. military officials have presented Trump with options for degrading Houthi military capabilities and stopping the rebels’ recent advances several times since Thursday, the official said, adding that the Pentagon has enough assets in the region to be ready to act if ordered to do so.

The New York Times reported some details of Trump’s decision-making process.

Violence escalated over the weekend, as the Houthis said they’d used missiles and drones on Saturday to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh and an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub.

The spokesperson for the coalition forces issued a statement on Saturday saying Saudi Arabia had successfully intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh and that the Houthis “target civilians and civilian infrastructure in the capital.”

The militant group also made a rapid advance to control the Bab el Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea, yet another oil chokepoint. The advance has posed a major challenge for the Saudis, who rely on that shipping route particularly since the Strait of Hormuz has been largely shuttered during the Iran war.

The Houthis took control of Yemen in a bloody civil war in 2014 against a Saudi-backed coalition. A fragile truce between the Houthis and the Yemeni government backed by the U.N. was reached in 2022.

Trump announced a ceasefire with the Houthis last year after weeks of punishing strikes against the militant group. Under the deal, the U.S. suspended military action and the Houthis stopped attacking U.S. ships.

Trump recently has said his administration has had discussions with the Houthis but has not offered details. “The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved.”

fullText:
Another leg up in gas prices to begin September underscores the political headwind that President Trump and Republicans face on the issue, with less than seven weeks left before the midterm elections.

The average price of US regular gasoline was $4.32 per gallon last Monday, according to the latest weekly data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA), a nearly $0.25 rise over the last two weeks.

The EIA data, which goes back to 1990, also shows that gas prices are the highest they've ever been at this stage in any recent election cycle, according to a Yahoo Finance analysis.

The second-highest price on record at this point — 49 days from an election — came in 2012 when gas cost $3.88 per gallon. The third-highest price was $3.65 in 2022. Both were election years when a Democratic administration was in power, and Republicans put a heavy focus on the issue of pump prices.

"Gas prices are at crazy levels--fire Obama!" then private citizen Donald Trump posted to social media back in 2012.

With Trump now in office, gas prices are being pushed up by a variety of factors, including both the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and they're hitting as Trump has few options to lower them due to widening disruptions in the Middle East and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at historically low levels after months of withdrawals.

Diesel, which broke through all-time high prices earlier this month and hit another record high last Tuesday, is yet another economic headwind.

The historical data also shows that prices tend to decline in the run-up to election day — in keeping with fall trends — but this year may be an outlier.

Nonpartisan energy analysts are downplaying the chances of significant price easing in the weeks or months ahead.

"In a typical year, the consumer would see a seasonal decline in gasoline prices as refiners switched from the more expensive summer grade gasoline to the less expensive winter grade formulation," Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, told Yahoo Finance.

But "this has been anything but a typical year," he said, noting that substantial price increases in gasoline and diesel could be felt across a range of consumer goods and are "wiping out the season savings that the consumer has come to expect."

GasBuddy's Patrick De Haan added in a recent blog post that the transition to cheaper winter-blend gasoline may help some, but "the scale of ongoing geopolitical escalations makes meaningful price relief unlikely in the near term."
